content:
Between a fully funded scholarship and paying your own way sits a gap that stops more UK master's dreams than any admission decision: tuition. GREAT Scholarships exist precisely for that gap. Each award is worth £10,000 towards tuition fees for a one-year taught postgraduate course, jointly funded by the UK government's GREAT Britain campaign, the British Council, and the participating university itself. In the current cycle more than 140 scholarships are on offer across over 60 universities in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

Who can apply: the 18 eligible countries

GREAT Scholarships are country-gated, and the list is aimed at the UK's priority growth markets: Bangladesh, China, Egypt, France, Ghana, Greece, India, Indonesia, Italy, Kenya, Malaysia, Mexico, Nigeria, Pakistan, Spain, Thailand, Turkey and Vietnam. If your passport is on that list, you can apply to any participating university's GREAT round for your country; if it is not, this scheme is unfortunately closed to you regardless of merit. Each country page on the British Council site lists the universities taking part for that nationality and the courses they attach the award to, which matters because a university may offer GREAT Scholarships to Pakistan but not to Vietnam in the same year.

What the money actually covers — and does not

Be clear-eyed about the arithmetic. A £10,000 award is substantial, but UK master's tuition for international students typically runs £18,000 to £35,000 depending on subject, and living costs add £12,000 to £15,000 for the year in most cities. GREAT is therefore a significant discount, not a ride: successful applicants either combine it with family funds, a partial fee waiver, or a smaller bursary from the same university. Read our honest breakdown of what self-funded study really costs before you commit, because the visa financial requirement still applies to the full balance.

How the application works

The mechanics vary slightly by university, but the pattern is consistent. You apply for admission to an eligible one-year taught master's first — the scholarship usually requires an offer, conditional or unconditional, before the award application is considered. Then you submit the university's GREAT scholarship form, which almost always includes an essay on how your studies will benefit your home country and your career. Deadlines are set per institution and mostly fall between February and June for September entry, though popular universities in some countries close earlier; the British Council country page is the reliable calendar.

How to win one

Because every award is judged by the university that funds it, the essay is really an admissions argument dressed as a scholarship essay. Committees look for three things: a course choice that visibly follows from your background, a realistic account of what you will do with it, and evidence you will contribute to the university community rather than merely consume it. Named modules, named employers, named problems. Our guide to the UK master's personal statement translates directly to this essay — the same discipline of specifics applies.

Two practical tips from past rounds. First, apply to more than one participating university: the awards are per-institution, so three applications triple your statistical chance for the same effort. Second, check whether your chosen course is actually in the university's GREAT list — business and law programmes are often excluded because demand is already high, while engineering, climate science and public health frequently are included. And if £10,000 is not enough of a dent for a PhD-level plan, remember that taught master's funding and doctoral funding are separate worlds — start with our UK PhD funding guide for the doctoral picture.

Combining GREAT with other funding

GREAT Scholarships stack in ways fully funded schemes do not, and planning for that changes your strategy. Because the award is a tuition contribution, universities sometimes allow it alongside their own international bursaries — an automatic £2,000 to £5,000 merit discount plus GREAT can bring fees near domestic levels at some institutions. What you cannot rely on is stacking it with a fully funded award like Chevening or Commonwealth for the same course; those schemes require you to declare other awards, and taking a full scholarship voids the GREAT payment. Read each university's terms page, because stacking rules differ and the British Council country page does not track them.

There is also a subject-strategy angle. Universities tend to attach GREAT awards to faculties they want to grow — engineering, health, climate and data-heavy programmes appear far more often than mainstream business courses. If your career allows flexibility between adjacent courses at the same university, choosing the one on the GREAT list rather than the one that merely exists is a £10,000 decision made before you even write the essay.

More UK funding in the £10,000 neighbourhood

A GREAT award rarely covers everything, so treat it as one layer of a funding stack. These live listings pair well with it — two of them consider you automatically, which means zero extra paperwork.

  • International PG Merit Scholarship 2027 at UEA — partial master’s funding with a rolling deadline
  • Vice Chancellor's Global Impact and Leadership Scholarship 2027 at UEA — UEA's flagship leadership scholarship. Deadline: 30 October 2026.
  • Durham University – Inspiring Excellence Scholarships (International) — Durham merit awards with automatic consideration
  • Interdisciplinary Chancellors Scholarships at University of Warwick 2027 — Warwick's cross-faculty PhD competition. Deadline: 10 December 2026, 16:59 GMT (course: 7 December; references: 21 December).
  • Leeds Doctoral Scholarship 2027 — Leeds' central doctoral scholarship competition. Deadline: 23 March 2027, 17:00 UK time.
  • AHRC Arts and Humanities PhD Scholarships, Sussex 2027 — Sussex AHRC awards for arts and humanities. Deadline: 10 December 2026, 16:00 GMT.
